bid.short: The highest price a buyer will pay right now. When you sell straight away, you sell at the bid.
bid.example: Bid $49.95, ask $50.05: sell now and you get $49.95.

ask.short: The lowest price a seller will accept right now. When you buy straight away, you buy at the ask.
ask.example: Bid $49.95, ask $50.05: buy now and you pay $50.05.

spread.short: The gap between the bid and the ask. You pay it on every round trip, even if the price never moves.
spread.long: Buy at the ask, sell at the bid, and the spread is gone. It works like a toll booth on every buy-and-sell. Busy markets have tight spreads; thin ones have wide spreads.
spread.example: Ask $50.05 − bid $49.95 = $0.10. On 100 shares a round trip costs $10.

liquidity.short: How easily you can buy or sell without moving the price. Liquid markets have many orders and tight spreads.
liquidity.example: A busy stock: bid $99.99, ask $100.01. A thin new coin: bid $0.095, ask $0.105, about a 10% toll.

bull-market.short: A sustained rise, often defined as about 20% or more up from a recent low. A bull expects prices to rise.
bull-market.long: Bulls toss their horns up: a bullish trader expects a rise. Measure in percent from the last low, not in points.
bull-market.example: An index rises from a low of 100 to 124: +24%, a bull market.

bear-market.short: A sustained fall, often defined as about 20% or more down from a recent high. A bear expects prices to fall.
bear-market.long: Bears swipe their paws down. One red week isn’t a bear market: measure the fall in percent from the last high.
bear-market.example: An index falls from a high of 4,000 to 3,400: −15%, not a bear market yet. It would need to reach about 3,200.

bullish.short: Expecting prices to rise. Like a bull tossing its horns up.
bullish.added: Not in the book; written for the Academy

bearish.short: Expecting prices to fall. Like a bear swiping its paws down.
bearish.added: Not in the book; written for the Academy

market-maker.short: A firm that is always ready to buy and sell, quoting both a bid and an ask. It earns the spread between them.
market-maker.long: Market makers keep markets moving. Your move against them: pay as little of the spread as you can.
market-maker.added: Definition written for the Academy (the book explains the idea in Chapter 1 but has no glossary entry)

asset-class.short: A family of things you can trade that behave alike: bonds, stocks, commodities, forex and crypto. Broad index ETFs count as a sixth group here: a basket that can hold any of them.
asset-class.long: From calmer to wilder: bonds and broad index ETFs, then stocks, commodities and forex, then crypto. Leverage makes any of them wilder. More possible reward usually means a wilder ride.
asset-class.added: Definition written for the Academy (the book explains the idea in Chapter 1 but has no glossary entry)

volatility.short: How much and how fast a price swings. Higher volatility means bigger moves, both up and down.
volatility.example: A calm market might move 1% a day; a wild one up to 15%. On $1,000 that’s $10 versus $150.

round-trip.short: One buy plus one sell of the same position. Costs like the spread and commission are counted per round trip.
round-trip.added: Not in the book; written for the Academy

etf.short: Exchange-traded fund: a basket of many assets that trades like a single stock. It’s as risky as what it holds; a broad index ETF is a calm place to start.

bond.short: A loan to a government or company. It pays interest and sits at the calm end of the risk ladder.
bond.added: Definition written for the Academy (the book explains the idea in Chapter 1 but has no glossary entry)

index.short: A number that tracks a group of stocks, like the S&P 500. It shows how the whole group is doing.
index.added: Not in the book; written for the Academy

hft.short: Robots that trade in millionths of a second. Their edge is speed, so don’t race them on tiny moves.
hft.added: Definition written for the Academy (the book explains the idea in Chapter 1 but has no glossary entry)

market-order.short: An order to trade right now at the best available price. You get speed, not a set price.
market-order.example: Price falling fast from $50, now $49.60: a market sell gets you out at about $49.60.

limit-order.short: An order to trade only at your price or better. You get your price, but it may never fill.
limit-order.example: Stock at $100, buy limit at $95: you buy only if it dips to $95 or lower.

stop-order.short: An order that waits for a trigger price, then becomes a market order. A buy stop sits above the price, a sell stop below.
stop-order.example: Stock at $30, buy stop at $32: it fires only if $32 trades.
stop-order.added: Definition written for the Academy (the book explains the idea in Chapter 2 but has no glossary entry)

stop-loss.short: An order that closes a trade at a pre-set loss level. Set it the moment you open the trade.
stop-loss.example: Own at $100, sell stop at $92: your loss is about $8 a share, unless the price gaps past your stop.

stop-limit.short: “When the price hits X, place a limit order at Y.” It controls your price, but in a crash it may not fill at all.
stop-limit.added: Definition written for the Academy (the book explains the idea in Chapter 2 but has no glossary entry)

long.short: Buying to profit from a rise: buy first, sell later. Result = (sell price − buy price) × shares.

short.short: Selling borrowed shares to profit from a fall, then buying them back. A short’s loss has no ceiling.
short.example: Sell 100 at $80, buy back at $70: +$1,000. If it rises to $90 instead: −$1,000.

squeeze.short: A fast rise in a heavily shorted stock as short sellers rush to buy back. Prices have doubled in days.
squeeze.added: Definition written for the Academy (the book explains the idea in Chapter 2 but has no glossary entry)

leverage.short: Controlling a bigger position than your money, using borrowed funds. It multiplies gains, losses and stress.
leverage.long: Position = margin × leverage. The move that wipes out your margin = 100% ÷ leverage: 10% at 10×, 5% at 20×, 1% at 100×.
leverage.example: $1,000 at 10× controls $10,000. A 10% fall takes all $1,000. US stock accounts allow about 2×; 10× and more is for forex, CFDs, futures and crypto.

margin.short: The deposit needed to open a leveraged position. Position = margin × leverage.

margin-call.short: A demand from your broker to add money when losses eat into your margin. It comes before your margin is gone, and the broker may close your trade.
margin-call.example: $10,000 stock position, $5,000 of your own, 25% maintenance: the call comes near $66.67, a 33% fall. At 10× it comes far sooner.

commission.short: A broker’s fee per trade or per share. Often zero now, but “free” brokers may earn it back through wider spreads.
commission.added: Definition written for the Academy (the book explains the idea in Chapter 2 but has no glossary entry)

slippage.short: The gap between the price you expected and the price you got. Biggest in fast markets and with market orders. Now and then it goes your way.
slippage.example: You tap Buy at $10.00 and fill at $10.08: $0.08 × 100 shares = $8.

swap.short: Overnight financing on a leveraged forex or CFD position, usually a cost, sometimes a small credit. On US stock margin it’s called margin interest.
swap.added: Definition written for the Academy (the book explains the idea in Chapter 2 but has no glossary entry)

gap.short: When a price opens far from the previous close, with no trades in between. A gap can jump straight past your stop.
gap.example: Close $50, stop $48, open $45: the stop fills near $45, not $48.

position-size.short: How much you buy. Size it so a stop-out or a normal gap costs a small, fixed share of your account.

earnings.short: A company’s profit, reported every quarter. Earnings day often brings big price moves and overnight gaps.
earnings.added: Not in the book; written for the Academy

correction.short: A fall of about 10% from a recent high. Smaller than a bear market, which is about 20% or more.
correction.example: From a high of 100: 90 is a correction, 80 is a bear market.
correction.added: Definition written for the Academy (Chapter 1 v2, Go deeper “Why 20%?”)

trading-plan.short: Your written rules for trading: your style and markets, when you enter, where you exit, how much you risk, your checklist and your weekly review.
trading-plan.example: Swing trading 4 markets, 1% risk a trade, a 6-check checklist, a review every Friday.

trading-style.short: How long you hold a trade: day trading (minutes to hours), swing trading (days to weeks) or position trading (weeks to months).
trading-style.example: You work 9 to 5 and have 30 minutes each evening: swing trading fits your time.

day-trading.short: Trades held for minutes to hours and all closed by the bell. It needs hours at the screen while the market is open.

swing-trading.short: Trades held for days to weeks. You check them about once a day, often after the close.

position-trading.short: Trades held for weeks to months. You check them about once a week.

entry-rule.short: One sentence that says exactly what must happen before you buy, so you can follow it the same way every time.
entry-rule.example: Buy when a rising stock pulls back to its rising 50-day average and closes back above it.

loss-limit.short: A circuit breaker: once you lose this much in a day or a week, you stop trading until the next day or week.
loss-limit.example: On $10,000: stop for the day at −2% ($200), for the week at −5% ($500).

pre-trade-checklist.short: 5 to 7 yes/no checks you run before every trade. Each check is a fact. One “no” means no trade.
pre-trade-checklist.example: My stop is set before I buy: yes. My target is at least 2× the risk: no. Skip it.

trading-journal.short: A record of every trade: the setup, entry, stop, target, result and how you felt. You read it in your weekly review.

weekly-review.short: Once a week you read your journal: did you follow every rule, your wins and losses, your biggest mistake, and one change or none.
weekly-review.example: Friday, 30 minutes with the journal: one change, then test it over 20 trades or more.

interest-rate.short: The price of borrowing money. The central bank sets the key rate; when it rises, loans cost more and cash pays more.
interest-rate.example: Rates go from 4% to 4.5%: loans get dearer, savings pay more, and stocks often fall.

central-bank.short: The bank that sets a country’s key interest rate, like the Federal Reserve in the US. It raises rates to cool inflation and cuts them to support growth.
central-bank.example: Inflation runs hot, so the central bank raises rates to slow spending.

inflation.short: How fast prices rise. Most countries track it with the CPI.
inflation.example: A basket that cost $100 last year costs $104 now: 4% inflation.

cpi.short: The Consumer Price Index: the cost of a basket of everyday goods, used to measure inflation. A monthly, high-impact release.
cpi.example: Markets expected 3%, CPI showed 4%: hotter than expected, so rates may stay higher for longer.

real-return.short: Your return minus inflation: what your money can actually buy.
real-return.example: A bond pays 6%, inflation is 4%: real return 6% − 4% = 2%.

economic-calendar.short: A list of when key economic data comes out, such as the jobs report, CPI and rate decisions, with each release’s expected impact.
economic-calendar.example: Wed 8:30 · CPI inflation · High: a day to cut size if you trade short-term.

sector.short: A group of companies in the same line of business, such as tech, energy, utilities or consumer staples.
sector.example: Oil rises 20%: the energy sector feels it most directly.

economic-cycle.short: The way economies grow, slow, shrink and recover. Some sectors have tended to do better in certain phases, but every cycle is different.
economic-cycle.example: In a slowdown, staples and utilities often hold up.

priced-in.short: Already reflected in the price. If everyone expected the news, the price has likely moved already, so the news itself barely moves it.
priced-in.example: A rate cut expected for weeks arrives; stocks rise just 0.1%.

share.short: A slice of ownership in a company. Owners share in its profits and usually get a vote.
share.example: 100 shares in total and you own 5: you own 5% of the company.
share.added: Definition written for the Academy from the Chapter 7 lessons

dividend.short: Part of a company’s profit paid out to its owners, the shareholders. Not every company pays one.
dividend.added: Definition written for the Academy from the Chapter 7 lessons

market-cap.short: What the market says a whole company is worth: share price × all the shares. Also called market cap.
market-cap.added: Definition written for the Academy from the Chapter 7 lessons

revenue.short: All the money a company takes in from sales, before any costs.
revenue.example: Acme sells $100M a year: its revenue is $100M.
revenue.added: Definition written for the Academy from the Chapter 7 lessons

profit.short: What’s left of revenue after every cost is paid.
profit.added: Definition written for the Academy from the Chapter 7 lessons

profit-margin.short: Profit ÷ revenue: how much of each dollar of sales the company keeps.
profit-margin.added: Definition written for the Academy from the Chapter 7 lessons

eps.short: A company’s profit ÷ its number of shares.
eps.added: Definition written for the Academy from the Chapter 7 lessons

pe-ratio.short: Share price ÷ EPS: how many dollars buyers pay for $1 of yearly profit. A high P/E means high expectations.
pe-ratio.added: Definition written for the Academy from the Chapter 7 lessons

cash-flow.short: The money that really came in, minus what really went out. Bills are paid in cash, not in profit.
cash-flow.added: Definition written for the Academy from the Chapter 7 lessons

earnings-estimate.short: The expected numbers analysts publish before results. Above it is a beat, below it a miss; the price moves on the gap.
earnings-estimate.added: Definition written for the Academy from the Chapter 7 lessons

guidance.short: What a company says it expects next, such as next year’s sales. It often moves the price more than the results.
guidance.example: Revenue and EPS beat, guidance cut: the price fell 6%.
guidance.added: Definition written for the Academy from the Chapter 7 lessons

diversification.short: Spreading money across many holdings, so one bad pick hurts a little, not a lot.
diversification.example: $1,000 in each of 10 stocks: if one falls 50%, you lose $500, just 5% of your money.

correlation.short: How two assets move together, from −1 (opposite) to +1 (in lockstep). Assets that rise and fall as one don’t protect each other.
correlation.example: Five big tech stocks tend to fall together in a tech sell-off: high correlation, little protection.

asset-allocation.short: How you split money between stocks, bonds and cash. For most people it matters more than any single pick.
asset-allocation.example: An example split: 60% stocks, 30% bonds, 10% cash. The right split depends on your goal and time.

rebalancing.short: Bringing your split back to its target: trim what grew, top up what lagged. Once or twice a year is enough for most people.
rebalancing.example: Target 60/40, now $8,000 stocks and $3,000 bonds: sell $1,400 of stocks, buy $1,400 of bonds.

benchmark.short: An index that matches what you hold. It’s the bar your results must clear, after all costs.
benchmark.example: You made 8%, a broad stock index made 15%: you lagged your benchmark by 7 points.

drawdown.short: The fall from a peak in your account or portfolio to the lowest point after it.
drawdown.example: $12,000 down to $8,400 is a 30% drawdown. A 50% drawdown needs a 100% gain to get back.

one-percent-rule.short: Risk at most about 1% (up to 2%) of your account on any one trade: the loss if your stop is hit, not the size of the position.
one-percent-rule.long: Losing streaks are normal, even for good strategies. At 1% a trade, 10 losses in a row leave you down about 10%. At 10% a trade, the same streak takes about two-thirds of the account.
one-percent-rule.example: Account $25,000 × 1% = $250 at most lost on one trade.

reward-to-risk.short: What a trade could make compared with what it could lose: (target − entry) ÷ (entry − stop). Pros aim for 2:1 or more.
reward-to-risk.long: The better the reward-to-risk, the fewer trades you need to win to break even: 50% at 1:1, 33% at 2:1, 25% at 3:1. The target must sit before resistance, or the ratio is only on paper.

expectancy.short: What a strategy makes per trade, on average, over many trades: (win rate × average win) − (loss rate × average loss).
expectancy.long: Above zero, the strategy pays over many trades; below zero, it loses. It says nothing sure about the next trade, and it needs a big sample (100+ trades, after fees) before you trust it.
expectancy.example: Win 40%, average win $300, average loss $100: (0.4 × $300) − (0.6 × $100) = +$60 a trade.

win-rate.short: The share of your trades that make money. On its own it says little: a high win rate can hide a losing strategy.
win-rate.example: Win 70% of trades at $50 but lose $150 on the rest: 0.7 × $50 − 0.3 × $150 = −$10 a trade.

fear-and-greed.short: The two feelings behind most trading mistakes. Fear closes winners early and skips good setups; greed trades too big and holds past the target.
fear-and-greed.long: Every trader feels them. The problem is letting them make the decisions. The defense is a plan made while you’re calm: entry, stop and target set before you trade.
fear-and-greed.example: Closing a winner at +$50 when the plan’s target was +$300 is fear. Holding a loser to −$150 past a −$50 stop is hope.

revenge-trading.short: Rushing into a bigger trade to win back a loss. It usually turns one bad trade into a bad day.
revenge-trading.example: Down $300, you double your size on a so-so setup. One more loss costs $600, and the day ends at −$900.

tilt.short: The angry state after a loss that drives revenge trading: bigger size, faster trades, setups you’d normally skip. Poker players named it.
tilt.example: Rule against tilt: 2 losses in a day and you’re done. Close the app; tomorrow is a new day.

fomo.short: Fear of missing out: the itch to jump in because a price is flying and everyone else is in. It makes you buy after the move, not before it.
fomo.example: Plan: buy $50, stop $48. Chasing at $56 with the same stop risks $8 a share instead of $2, four times the plan.

loss-aversion.short: A loss hurts about twice as much as an equal gain feels good. It tempts you to hold losers and sell winners early.
loss-aversion.example: Most people turn down a fair coin flip: heads +$100, tails −$100. The odds are even; the feelings are not.

candlestick.short: One bar on a price chart that shows four prices for its period: open, high, low and close. Green closed above its open, red below.
candlestick.example: A green daily candle: open $100, high $108, low $97, close $105.

ohlc.short: The four prices in every candle: where the period started, its highest and lowest price, and where it ended.
ohlc.example: Open $50, high $51, low $45, close $46: a red candle.

wick.short: The thin line above or below a candle’s body. It reaches the high or the low: how far price went before it was pushed back.
wick.example: Body tops out at $105, upper wick reaches $108: price touched $108 but closed at $105.

hammer.short: A candle with a small body near the top and a long lower wick, after a fall. Buyers fought back from the lows.
hammer.example: Low $90, close $97.50 after four down days: buyers pushed price back up $7.50.

doji.short: A candle that opens and closes at almost the same price. Neither buyers nor sellers won: indecision.
doji.example: Open $80, close $80 after a 10-day rise: a clue to watch, not a sell signal.

engulfing.short: A candle whose body swallows the whole body of the one before it. Bullish engulfing: after a fall, a big green body swallows a red one.
engulfing.example: Red candle $93.20 → $92, then green opens at $91.60 and closes at $95.80.

timeframe.short: How much time one candle covers: 1 minute, 1 hour, 1 day or 1 week. Same stock, same prices, different story.
timeframe.example: Holding for weeks? Trade from the daily chart and check the weekly first.

volume.short: How many shares changed hands in a period. Moves on high volume have more people behind them; volume shows strength, not direction.
volume.example: Normal day 1M shares; a breakout on 3M is more believable than one on 0.5M.

support.short: A price zone where buyers stepped in before: a floor. It’s a zone, not an exact line, and broken support often turns into resistance.
support.example: Price bounced near $40 three times: $40 is support. A stop goes a little below, near $38.

resistance.short: A price zone where sellers stepped in before: a ceiling. Once it breaks, it often turns into support.
resistance.example: Price stalled near $48 twice: $48 is resistance, a place to plan a target.

breakout.short: When price moves through a level it couldn’t pass before, such as above resistance. More believable on high volume.
breakout.example: A break above $50 on 3× normal volume beats one on half the usual volume.

uptrend.short: A market making higher highs and higher lows. It lasts until that pattern breaks.

downtrend.short: A market making lower highs and lower lows.

sideways.short: A market with no new highs or lows: price bounces between a floor and a ceiling.
sideways.example: Three months between $20 and $24 without breaking out: a range.

swing.short: A peak or a dip on a chart. Compare each swing with the last to read the trend.
swing.example: Higher high (HH), higher low (HL), lower high (LH), lower low (LL).

trendline.short: A straight line under at least two rising lows (or over two falling highs), extended to the right. A break is a warning, not a signal.
trendline.example: Line at $47.80, close $47.20: about 1% below. Watch the next highs and lows.

channel.short: A trendline plus a parallel line through the highs. Price often travels between the two, like a lane.
channel.example: Near the lower line buyers often step in; near the upper line sellers do.

moving-average.short: The average close of the last N days, redrawn each day. It smooths price into one line and lags: it turns after price does.

double-top.short: Two failed tries at the same high. Confirmed only on a close below the middle low between them.
double-top.example: Peaks $80 and $80, middle low $72: a close below $72 confirms it; rough target $64.

double-bottom.short: Two failed tries at the same low. Confirmed only on a close above the middle high between them.
double-bottom.example: Lows $50 and $50, middle high $56: a close above $56 confirms it; rough target $62.

head-and-shoulders.short: Three peaks: a left shoulder, a higher head and a lower right shoulder. It counts only on a close through the neckline.

neckline.short: The line joining the lows between the peaks of a head and shoulders. A close through it confirms the pattern.
neckline.example: Neckline $27: the pattern is confirmed on a close below $27.

rsi.short: A 0–100 speed gauge comparing recent up days with recent down days, usually over 14 days. It measures speed, not value.
rsi.example: RSI 75: price rose fast. In a strong uptrend it can stay above 70 for weeks.

overbought.short: RSI above 70: price rose fast. Fast isn’t finished, so it isn’t a sell signal on its own.
overbought.example: Selling the first time RSI hit 70 meant missing the next 24%.

oversold.short: RSI below 30: price fell fast. It can keep falling, so it isn’t a buy signal on its own.
oversold.example: RSI 25: price has fallen fast lately.

macd.short: The gap between a fast (12-day) and a slow (26-day) exponential average. A 9-day signal line and bars show momentum building or fading.
macd.example: Fast average $52 − slow average $50 = +2: above zero.

confluence.short: Several different kinds of evidence agreeing, like trend, level and volume. Indicators built from the same prices don’t count twice.
confluence.example: Uptrend, a bounce at $58 support, 2× normal volume: confluence.
